memoryText: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Romans 1:16 slowly, several times, and try to say it from memory. Then read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Paul writes this verse at the start of the greatest explanation of the gospel ever written.

“I am not ashamed of the gospel.” Paul says this because the gospel is easy to be ashamed of. It speaks of a crucified Savior, which seemed foolish to Greeks and offensive to Jews. It tells us we are sinners who cannot save ourselves. The world’s wisdom has not changed. And yet Paul is not ashamed. His boldness does not come from temperament but from conviction.

“For it is the power of God for salvation.” The gospel is not only information or a good idea. It is the power of God, the means by which he saves. When it is preached, God works. Dead hearts are raised, and enemies become children.

“To everyone who believes.” The gospel has a condition that is not a work: believing. It rests on Christ and not on us. It is open to all.

“To the Jew first and also to the Greek.” The gospel came to Israel first, and the promises were theirs. But it goes beyond to every nation. In Romans, Paul will show how Jew and Gentile are saved the same way.

When you are tempted to be quiet about your faith, say this verse. The power does not rest in your ability to explain, but in the gospel itself.
weekInReview: This week you began Paul’s letter to the Romans, the great explanation of the new covenant. You read the opening greeting and the statement of the theme: the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, and in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith. Then Paul gave the bad news that makes the good news necessary. God’s wrath is revealed against all who suppress the truth, and he gives them up to the consequences of their sin. In a doctrinal pause, you thought about the wrath of God as his holy opposition to evil, and with Nahum you saw that the same God is a stronghold to those who take refuge in him. In chapter 2, Paul turned to the moral and religious person: God judges impartially, his kindness is meant to lead to repentance, and a true Jew is one inwardly, circumcised in heart by the Spirit.
reflectionQuestions: Paul says he is not ashamed of the gospel. In what setting, with which people, are you most tempted to be ashamed or silent about Christ? What would it look like to speak with quiet confidence there?
Romans 1 and 2 show that everyone, religious or not, is guilty before God. How does the cross of Jesus, where he bore the wrath we deserved, change the way you feel when you read these chapters?
Paul says God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance. Where is God’s kindness leading you to turn right now?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the gospel, the power for salvation.
Ask him to keep you from shame and make you bold.
